title: What Is Disruptive Innovation?
author_source: Christensen, C.M., Raynor, M.E., McDonald, R.; Harvard Business Review, Dec 2015; practitioner article
note: Christensen's own 20-year restatement: low-end vs new-market footholds, why Uber is NOT disruptive under the theory, and the 'disruption is a process' clarification. Ideal for correcting the loose everyday use of 'disruption'. About 10 pages, includes the classic performance-trajectory chart.
course_use: Core reading for the session on innovation types; in-class exercise: classify Uber, Netflix, Tesla, Dacia with the article's tests. HBR paywall, WU access via EBSCO Business Source (WU-Lizenz prüfen).

title: Disruptive Innovation: An Intellectual History and Directions for Future Research
author_source: Christensen, C.M., McDonald, R., Altman, E.J., Palmer, J.E.; Journal of Management Studies 55(7), 2018; review article
note: Academic counterpart to the HBR piece: traces how the theory moved from a technology-change framework (disk drives) to a causal theory of competitive response, lists anomalies that refined it and open questions (incumbent responses, performance trajectories, metrics). Good for Master/PhD-level depth.
course_use: Master/MBA reading or background for the lecturer; pair with the King and Baatartogtokh critique for a debate. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: How Useful Is the Theory of Disruptive Innovation?
author_source: King, A.A., Baatartogtokh, B.; MIT Sloan Management Review 57(1), Fall 2015; empirical critique
note: Surveyed 79 industry experts on the 77 cases Christensen and Raynor used: only 7 (about 9 percent) showed all four core elements of the theory. Short, data-based critique that students can read in 20 minutes; the case table is directly usable for discussion.
course_use: Debate session: half the class defends Christensen (HBR 2015), half uses this critique. SMR paywall (a few free articles per month), WU-Lizenz prüfen via EBSCO.

title: The Disruption Machine: What the gospel of innovation gets wrong
author_source: Lepore, J.; The New Yorker, 23 June 2014; essay/critique
note: The most-cited public critique: questions case selection (e.g. disk drives, steel) and the theory's predictive power, and frames 'disruption' as ideology. Rhetorically strong, less rigorous than King and Baatartogtokh; useful to show that management theories are contested.
course_use: Optional reading for the disruption debate; Bachelor-level warm-up. New Yorker metered paywall.

title: Disruptive Innovation: In Need of Better Theory
author_source: Markides, C.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 23(1), 2006; conceptual article
note: Argues that disruptive technological, business-model and radical product innovations are distinct phenomena with different competitive effects and incumbent responses. Short (about 8 pages) and very clear; good bridge between disruption and the radical/incremental typology.
course_use: Reading for the innovation-types session (Master); use its typology as a classification exercise. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Disruptive Technology Reconsidered: A Critique and Research Agenda
author_source: Danneels, E.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 21(4), 2004; critique
note: Early academic critique: problems in defining disruptive technology ex ante, hindsight bias in case selection, and whether disruption can be predicted. Complements King and Baatartogtokh with conceptual arguments.
course_use: Master seminar reading or background for lecturer. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: The Effects of Mainstream and Emerging Customer Orientations on Radical and Disruptive Innovations
author_source: Govindarajan, V., Kopalle, P.K., Danneels, E.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 28(s1), 2011; empirical (128 SBUs of Fortune 200 firms)
note: Empirical test that separates radical from disruptive innovation: mainstream customer orientation helps radical but hurts disruptive innovation; willingness to cannibalize drives disruptive innovation. Makes the 'listen to your customers' paradox of the innovator's dilemma testable.
course_use: Master reading on the innovator's dilemma; discussion question: should firms listen to their customers? WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: A critical look at technological innovation typology and innovativeness terminology: a literature review
author_source: Garcia, R., Calantone, R.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 19(2), 2002; review
note: Standard reference for definitions: radical vs really new vs incremental innovation, macro vs micro perspective, new-to-world vs new-to-firm. Useful to fix terminology at the start of the course; includes a classification table.
course_use: Background/definitions reading for the first session (Bachelor and Master). WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms
author_source: Henderson, R.M., Clark, K.B.; Administrative Science Quarterly 35(1), 1990; classic empirical/conceptual article
note: Introduces the 2x2 of incremental, modular, architectural and radical innovation (component vs architectural knowledge), illustrated with photolithographic aligners. Still the standard explanation for why incumbents fail at seemingly minor innovations.
course_use: Classic reading (Master/MBA); use the 2x2 in class to classify current products (e.g. e-bikes, smartphones). JSTOR, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Organizing for Radical Product Innovation: The Overlooked Role of Willingness to Cannibalize
author_source: Chandy, R.K., Tellis, G.J.; Journal of Marketing Research 35(4), 1998; empirical
note: Marketing classic showing that willingness to cannibalize own investments is a key driver of radical product innovation, more than firm size. Provides a clear technology-vs-customer-need definition of radical innovation (2x2).
course_use: Master reading on radical innovation; links to the innovator's dilemma. WU-Lizenz prüfen (SAGE/JSTOR).

title: The Incumbent's Curse? Incumbency, Size, and Radical Product Innovation
author_source: Chandy, R.K., Tellis, G.J.; Journal of Marketing 64(3), 2000; empirical (historical data on 64 radical innovations)
note: Challenges the 'incumbent's curse': after WWII, large incumbents introduced a growing share of radical innovations. Good counterpoint to the innovator's dilemma for class debate.
course_use: Debate reading paired with Christensen; Master/MBA. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Radical Innovation across Nations: The Preeminence of Corporate Culture
author_source: Tellis, G.J., Prabhu, J.C., Chandy, R.K.; Journal of Marketing 73(1), 2009; empirical (759 firms, 17 nations)
note: Shows that corporate culture (willingness to cannibalize, future focus, risk tolerance) predicts radical innovation better than country factors; includes measurable culture items. Useful for an Austrian/European perspective on innovation capability.
course_use: Master reading; students can apply the culture items to a company they know. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Sources and Financial Consequences of Radical Innovation: Insights from Pharmaceuticals
author_source: Sorescu, A.B., Chandy, R.K., Prabhu, J.C.; Journal of Marketing 67(4), 2003; empirical
note: Shows that dominant firms introduce more radical drug innovations and that radical innovations create substantial firm value, especially with strong marketing and technology support. Good evidence for 'why innovate' in marketing terms.
course_use: Master/MBA reading on innovation and firm value. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Do Innovations Really Pay Off? Total Stock Market Returns to Innovation
author_source: Sorescu, A., Spanjol, J.; Marketing Science 28(5), 2009; empirical (CPG innovations)
note: Long-term stock market returns of breakthrough vs incremental consumer packaged goods innovations: breakthroughs pay off, incremental ones largely do not. Concrete, finance-linked evidence for the innovation-type discussion.
course_use: Master/MBA reading; use the results for a portfolio-strategy discussion. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Product Innovations, Advertising, and Stock Returns
author_source: Srinivasan, S., Pauwels, K., Silva-Risso, J., Hanssens, D.M.; Journal of Marketing 73(1), 2009; empirical (US automotive)
note: Firm value rises with pioneering innovations and with advertising support for them; minor updates add little. Links innovation types to launch marketing, a bridge to the go-to-market session.
course_use: Master/MBA reading; good for a launch-budget discussion. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: A New Product Growth for Model Consumer Durables
author_source: Bass, F.M.; Management Science 15(5), 1969; classic model article
note: The original Bass diffusion model with innovation (p) and imitation (q) coefficients, fitted to 11 consumer durables. Short and still the basis of every forecasting exercise; the 2004 reprint with Bass's own comments (Management Science 50(12), doi 10.1287/mnsc.1040.0300) explains its later uses.
course_use: Background for the Bass forecasting lab (Excel or R); Bachelor students read the 2004 commentary instead. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: New Product Diffusion Models in Marketing: A Review and Directions for Research
author_source: Mahajan, V., Muller, E., Bass, F.M.; Journal of Marketing 54(1), 1990; review
note: Classic review of Bass-type models: estimation, extensions with marketing-mix variables, multi-generation and repeat purchase. Contains typical p and q values useful for analogy-based forecasting.
course_use: Background for lecturer and Master students before the forecasting lab. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Innovation diffusion and new product growth models: A critical review and research directions
author_source: Peres, R., Muller, E., Mahajan, V.; International Journal of Research in Marketing 27(2), 2010; review
note: Most-used modern review: extends diffusion beyond word of mouth to network externalities and social signals, covers cross-country diffusion, competition and growth-stage phenomena (takeoff, saddle). Best single update since Mahajan et al. 1990.
course_use: Master reading for the adoption/forecasting block. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: Will It Ever Fly? Modeling the Takeoff of Really New Consumer Durables
author_source: Golder, P.N., Tellis, G.J.; Marketing Science 16(3), 1997; empirical
note: Models the time to sales takeoff across 31 really new consumer durables (on average about six years after introduction) and links takeoff to price declines. Useful facts for discussing why really new products need patience, alongside Moore's chasm.
course_use: Master reading; combine with Moore's Crossing the Chasm (book) in the adoption session. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Consumer Resistance to Innovations: The Marketing Problem and Its Solutions
author_source: Ram, S., Sheth, J.N.; Journal of Consumer Marketing 6(2), 1989; conceptual classic
note: Defines functional barriers (usage, value, risk) and psychological barriers (tradition, image) to adoption, with marketing remedies for each. Very teachable framework that complements Rogers' adoption factors.
course_use: Bachelor/Master reading; exercise: apply the barrier list to a current innovation (e.g. cultivated meat, smart glasses). WU-Lizenz prüfen (Emerald).

title: Consumer resistance to innovation - a behavioral reasoning perspective
author_source: Claudy, M.C., Garcia, R., O'Driscoll, A.; Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 43(4), 2015; empirical
note: Shows that 'reasons against' adoption are not simply the inverse of 'reasons for' (behavioral reasoning theory), tested on micro wind turbines. Good for sustainable-innovation adoption examples.
course_use: Master reading; supports a lab where students collect reasons for/against an innovation. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer).

title: Innovations - Doomed to Fail? Investigating Strategies to Overcome Passive Innovation Resistance
author_source: Heidenreich, S., Kraemer, T.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 33(3), 2016; experiments
note: German authors distinguish passive (status-quo, inclination to resist change) from active resistance and test communication strategies to overcome it. Directly applicable to launch messaging.
course_use: Master reading for the adoption and launch sessions. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Entrenched Knowledge Structures and Consumer Response to New Products
author_source: Moreau, C.P., Lehmann, D.R., Markman, A.B.; Journal of Marketing Research 38(1), 2001; experiments
note: Category experts understand really new products better but evaluate them less favourably (entrenched knowledge), while they favour continuous innovations. Explains why expert panels can misjudge radical concepts.
course_use: Master reading in the really-new-products / concept-testing block. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Measuring Preferences for Really New Products
author_source: Hoeffler, S.; Journal of Marketing Research 40(4), 2003; experiments
note: Shows that preference measurement for really new products is unstable because consumers lack relevant knowledge; mental simulation and analogies improve prediction. Key caution for concept tests and conjoint with radical products.
course_use: Master reading; link to the concept-testing lab (why standard surveys fail for really new products). WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Open Innovation: Research, Practices, and Policies
author_source: Bogers, M., Chesbrough, H., Moedas, C.; California Management Review 60(2), 2018; overview
note: Short, accessible update by Chesbrough (with EU commissioner Moedas) on what open innovation means 15 years on: inbound/outbound flows, firm practices and policy. Better first reading than the 2003 book.
course_use: Reading for the open-innovation session (Bachelor/Master). WU-Lizenz prüfen (SAGE).

title: How open is innovation?
author_source: Dahlander, L., Gann, D.M.; Research Policy 39(6), 2010; review
note: Classifies openness into four types (acquiring, sourcing, selling, revealing; pecuniary vs non-pecuniary) with benefits and costs. Practical 2x2 for analysing a firm's open innovation strategy; a 2021 retrospective exists (doi 10.1016/j.respol.2021.104218).
course_use: Master reading; students map a company (e.g. LEGO, Henkel) onto the four types. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: Lead Users: A Source of Novel Product Concepts
author_source: von Hippel, E.; Management Science 32(7), 1986; classic conceptual
note: Original definition of lead users (ahead of the trend, high expected benefit) and the steps of the lead-user process. Still the standard reference before any lead-user workshop.
course_use: Background reading for the idea-generation session. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Performance Assessment of the Lead User Idea-Generation Process for New Product Development
author_source: Lilien, G.L., Morrison, P.D., Searls, K., Sonnack, M., von Hippel, E.; Management Science 48(8), 2002; field study at 3M
note: Natural experiment at 3M: lead-user projects produced ideas with projected annual sales about 8 times higher than projects using traditional methods. The strongest quantitative evidence for the lead-user method and a good case story.
course_use: Master/MBA reading; pair with a lead-user search exercise in class. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: The Value of Crowdsourcing: Can Users Really Compete with Professionals in Generating New Product Ideas?
author_source: Poetz, M.K., Schreier, M.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 29(2), 2012; empirical (baby products)
note: Blind evaluation of user vs professional ideas for baby products: user ideas scored higher on novelty and customer benefit, somewhat lower on feasibility. Co-author Schreier is at WU Wien; highly cited and easy to replicate in class.
course_use: Core reading for crowdsourcing; replicate with a class ideation contest. Local guest-speaker link (WU). WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: User-generated versus designer-generated products: A performance assessment at Muji
author_source: Nishikawa, H., Schreier, M., Ogawa, S.; International Journal of Research in Marketing 30(2), 2013; field data
note: Real market data from Muji: user-generated products achieved about three times higher sales and five times higher gross margins than designer-generated ones in their first year. Strong evidence that crowdsourcing pays beyond lab ratings.
course_use: Master reading; use as a mini case on crowdsourcing at Muji. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: Consumer Cocreation in New Product Development
author_source: Hoyer, W.D., Chandy, R., Dorotic, M., Krafft, M., Singh, S.S.; Journal of Service Research 13(3), 2010; conceptual
note: Framework of co-creation across NPD stages (ideation, development, commercialization), with motivators and impediments for consumers and firms. Good structuring device for a session on customer integration.
course_use: Reading for the co-creation session (Bachelor/Master). WU-Lizenz prüfen (SAGE).

title: Customer Empowerment in New Product Development
author_source: Fuchs, C., Schreier, M.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 28(1), 2011; experiments
note: Shows that observing customers perceive firms that let customers create or vote on products more favourably (customer orientation, attitude, purchase intent). Useful for the marketing side of co-creation; WU-linked author.
course_use: Master reading; discussion: is co-creation a PR or an innovation tool? WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Artificial intelligence and its impact on creativity and diversity: An empirical study of LLM-generated product ideas (earlier SSRN title: Ideas are Dimes a Dozen: Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation)
author_source: Terwiesch, C., Meincke, L., Girotra, K., Mollick, E.; Production and Operations Management, 2026 (working paper Girotra et al. 2023); experiments
note: Published version of the much-cited Girotra et al. 2023 working paper: GPT-4 product ideas (college-student products under 50 USD) have higher purchase intent and are about 7 times more likely to be in the top 10 percent, but are less novel and less diverse; tests fixes (pooling models, chain-of-thought prompting, personas). Free SSRN version: doi 10.2139/ssrn.4526071.
course_use: Core reading for AI in innovation; replicate the task in a lab with ChatGPT vs student teams. SSRN version free; journal version WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance
author_source: Meincke, L., Mollick, E., Terwiesch, C.; Wharton working paper / SSRN / arXiv 2402.01727, 2024
note: Compares many prompting strategies for GPT-4 ideation; pools of AI ideas are less diverse than human groups, but chain-of-thought prompting nearly closes the gap. Short and practical; prompts are reusable by students.
course_use: Lab material: students test prompt strategies and measure idea overlap. Free on arXiv and SSRN.

title: The Crowdless Future? Generative AI and Creative Problem-Solving
author_source: Boussioux, L., Lane, J.N., Zhang, M., Jacimovic, V., Lakhani, K.R.; Organization Science 35(5), 2024; field experiment
note: Crowdsourcing challenge on circular-economy business ideas (234 solutions, 300 evaluators): human crowd solutions were more novel, human-AI solutions scored higher on value and overall quality; 'differentiated search' prompting performed best. Connects crowdsourcing (Poetz and Schreier) with GenAI and sustainability.
course_use: Master/MBA reading; debate whether AI replaces crowdsourcing. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS); SSRN preprint free (doi 10.2139/ssrn.4533642).

title: Augmenting Human Innovation Teams with Artificial Intelligence: Exploring Transformer-Based Language Models
author_source: Bouschery, S.G., Blazevic, V., Piller, F.T.; Journal of Product Innovation Management 40(2), 2023; conceptual
note: Maps LLM uses onto an AI-augmented double-diamond NPD process (problem and solution space exploration) and sets a research agenda; abstract written by GPT-3. German authors (RWTH Aachen); open access.
course_use: Bachelor/Master reading as a framework for AI across NPD stages. Open access (Wiley).

title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise
author_source: Dell'Acqua, F., Ayoubi, C., Lifshitz-Assaf, H., Sadun, R., Mollick, E., et al.; NBER Working Paper 33641, 2025; field experiment at Procter and Gamble
note: Field experiment with 776 Procter and Gamble professionals developing real product ideas: individuals with AI matched two-person teams without AI, and AI reduced R&D vs commercial silos. Best recent field evidence on GenAI in actual NPD work.
course_use: Master/MBA reading for the AI session; discussion of team design in NPD. Free via SSRN (doi 10.2139/ssrn.5188231); NBER may need subscription.

title: Generative AI in innovation and marketing processes: A roadmap of research opportunities
author_source: Cillo, P., Rubera, G.; Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 2024 (online); review/agenda
note: Structures how GenAI changes idea generation, product design and the marketing of innovations, with research questions per stage. Useful overview before the empirical AI ideation papers and as a thesis-topic source.
course_use: Master reading / thesis-topic source. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer; check for open access).

title: Why Some New Products Are More Successful than Others
author_source: Henard, D.H. & Szymanski, D.M., Journal of Marketing Research 38(3), 362-375, 2001, article (meta-analysis)
note: Meta-analysis of 24 predictors of new product performance; product advantage, market potential, meeting customer needs, predevelopment task proficiency and dedicated resources come out strongest. Shows how effects vary by measurement (subjective vs objective) and context (goods vs services). Effect-size table is a ready slide.
course_use: Core reading for the success-factors session (Bachelor/Master); paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Success Factors of Product Innovation: An Updated Meta-Analysis
author_source: Evanschitzky, H., Eisend, M., Calantone, R.J. & Jiang, Y., Journal of Product Innovation Management 29(S1), 21-37, 2012, article (meta-analysis)
note: Updates Henard & Szymanski with 233 studies and 2,618 effect sizes (1999-2011), random-effects model. Key teaching points: success-factor effects weaken over time, and national culture moderates them (stronger in uncertainty-avoiding countries, relevant for Austria/DACH).
course_use: Pair with Henard & Szymanski 2001: students compare which success factors held up; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Determinants of New Product Performance: A Review and Meta-Analysis
author_source: Montoya-Weiss, M.M. & Calantone, R., Journal of Product Innovation Management 11(5), 397-417, 1994, article (meta-analysis)
note: First meta-analysis of NPD performance (47 studies, 18 determinants grouped into strategic, development process, market environment and organizational factors). Useful for the history of the success-factor stream and its methodological critique.
course_use: Background reading for Master/PhD seminars; classic, paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Drivers of Success in New-Product Development
author_source: Cooper, R.G., Industrial Marketing Management 76, 36-47, 2019, article (review)
note: Synthesis of decades of NewProd research into 20 success drivers on three levels: project (voice of customer, front-end homework, compelling value proposition), business (innovation strategy, resources, climate) and systems/methods (gating, Agile, ideation). Practitioner-friendly language.
course_use: Very good first reading for Bachelor students, use as checklist for a case audit; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Best Practices in New Product Development and Innovation: Results from PDMA's 2021 Global Survey
author_source: Knudsen, M.P., von Zedtwitz, M., Griffin, A. & Barczak, G., Journal of Product Innovation Management 40(3), 257-275, 2023, article (survey study)
note: 651 companies in 37 countries; compares the Best with the Rest. No single practice explains top performance; for the first time a radical, risk-taking innovation strategy matters most. Provides current benchmarks (success rates, share of sales from new products) for KPI sessions.
course_use: Reading plus data source for an innovation-KPI exercise; published open access by Wiley/PDMA

title: Stage-Gate Systems: A New Tool for Managing New Products
author_source: Cooper, R.G., Business Horizons 33(3), 44-54, 1990, article
note: The original short description of Stage-Gate: stages, gates with must-meet and should-meet criteria, gatekeepers. Short (11 pages) and readable, still the standard reference for the process model.
course_use: Pre-reading before a Stage-Gate simulation or gate-review role play; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Agile-Stage-Gate Hybrids
author_source: Cooper, R.G., Research-Technology Management 59(1), 21-29, 2016, article
note: Practitioner article on how manufacturers combine sprints and scrums inside Stage-Gate development and testing stages; lists benefits and implementation problems with company examples. Good bridge from software agile to physical products.
course_use: Reading for the agile/hybrid session; pair with Cooper & Sommer 2016 JPIM; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Agile-Stage-Gate Hybrid Model: A Promising New Approach and a New Research Opportunity
author_source: Cooper, R.G. & Sommer, A.F., Journal of Product Innovation Management 33(5), 513-526, 2016, article
note: Academic version of the hybrid model with case evidence from early adopters (faster time to market, better response to changing customer needs) and a research agenda. Shows where agile and gating conflict (resource allocation, management role).
course_use: Master reading; good for a debate 'Is Stage-Gate dead?'; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Agile-Stage-Gate for Manufacturers: Changing the Way New Products Are Developed
author_source: Cooper, R.G. & Sommer, A.F., Research-Technology Management 61(2), 17-26, 2018, article
note: Focuses on manufacturing (non-software) firms and gives concrete practices: sprint length, incremental product versions shown to customers, co-located teams, role of gatekeepers. Includes reported performance gains from adopters.
course_use: Applied reading for MBA/executive groups from manufacturing; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Providing Clarity and a Common Language to the Fuzzy Front End
author_source: Koen, P. et al., Research-Technology Management 44(2), 46-55, 2001, article
note: Introduces the New Concept Development model (opportunity identification, opportunity analysis, idea genesis, idea selection, concept definition) and contrasts the fuzzy front end with structured NPD. The standard reference for the front end.
course_use: Reading for the front-end/ideation session; model works as a framework for student projects; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: How Ideation Portfolio Management Influences Front-End Success
author_source: Kock, A., Heising, W. & Gemünden, H.G., Journal of Product Innovation Management 32(4), 539-555, 2015, article
note: Survey of German firms showing that idea generation, idea screening and ideation portfolio management drive front-end success and later portfolio success. DACH evidence on managing the fuzzy front end systematically.
course_use: Master reading, DACH example for the front end; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: NPD Planning Activities and Innovation Performance: The Mediating Role of Process Management and the Moderating Effect of Product Innovativeness
author_source: Salomo, S., Weise, J. & Gemünden, H.G., Journal of Product Innovation Management 24(4), 285-302, 2007, article
note: 132 German NPD projects: project planning, risk planning and goal stability improve NPD performance, mediated by process management. DACH evidence that planning still pays off, a useful counterpoint to lean/agile enthusiasm.
course_use: Master seminar reading, discussion 'plan vs experiment'; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Mixed Blessings of Technological Innovativeness for the Commercial Success of New Products
author_source: Kock, A., Gemünden, H.G., Salomo, S. & Schultz, C., Journal of Product Innovation Management 28(S1), 28-43, 2011, article
note: Longitudinal, two-informant study of German NPD projects: technological innovativeness raises customer value but also creates internal and external change costs, so the net effect on success is close to zero. Good for discussing why radical products often disappoint.
course_use: Master reading, DACH research; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Design Thinking
author_source: Brown, T., Harvard Business Review 86(6), 84-92, June 2008, article (practitioner)
note: IDEO's CEO describes design thinking as human-centred, prototype-driven innovation (inspiration, ideation, implementation) with company examples. The canonical practitioner introduction.
course_use: Short reading or warm-up before a design-thinking workshop; HBR paywall, available via EBSCO Business Source (WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: Perspective: Linking Design Thinking with Innovation Outcomes through Cognitive Bias Reduction
author_source: Liedtka, J., Journal of Product Innovation Management 32(6), 925-938, 2015, article
note: Explains why design thinking should work: maps its tools (ethnography, prototyping, co-creation) to the cognitive biases they reduce (projection, egocentric empathy, confirmation bias). Provides a theory beyond the hype.
course_use: Master reading; pair with Brown 2008 to move from method to mechanism; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Doing Design Thinking: Conceptual Review, Synthesis, and Research Agenda
author_source: Micheli, P., Wilner, S.J.S., Bhatti, S.H., Mura, M. & Beverland, M.B., Journal of Product Innovation Management 36(2), 124-148, 2019, article (systematic review)
note: Systematic review identifying ten attributes of design thinking (e.g. creativity, user-centredness, abductive reasoning, iterative experimentation) and the tools used. Useful to define the concept precisely in student theses.
course_use: Master/thesis background reading; check OA status, otherwise WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Design, Meanings, and Radical Innovation: A Metamodel and a Research Agenda
author_source: Verganti, R., Journal of Product Innovation Management 25(5), 436-456, 2008, article
note: Design-driven innovation: radical innovation of product meanings (Italian design firms, Nintendo Wii) rather than user-centred incremental improvement. Counterpoint to design thinking and customer-led approaches.
course_use: Master reading; debate 'listen to users vs propose new meanings'; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Scientific Approach to Entrepreneurial Decision Making: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial
author_source: Camuffo, A., Cordova, A., Gambardella, A. & Spina, C., Management Science 66(2), 564-586, 2020, article (RCT)
note: RCT with 116 Italian startups: those trained to formulate theories and test hypotheses (lean-startup style experimentation done rigorously) perform better and pivot more without dropping out more. The best causal evidence that structured experimentation pays.
course_use: Key evidence for the lean startup / MVP session; also good for teaching RCT logic; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Scientific Approach to Entrepreneurial Decision-Making: Large-Scale Replication and Extension
author_source: Camuffo, A., Gambardella, A., Messinese, D., Novelli, E., Paolucci, E. & Spina, C., Strategic Management Journal 45(6), 1209-1237, 2024, article (4 RCTs)
note: Replication with 759 firms in four RCTs: the scientific approach mainly raises idea termination and leads to a few focused radical pivots rather than none or many. Useful to show replication and to nuance the 2020 result.
course_use: Follow-up reading for Master students; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Lean Startup Method: Early-Stage Teams and Hypothesis-Based Probing of Business Ideas
author_source: Leatherbee, M. & Katila, R., Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal 14(4), 570-593, 2020, article
note: Study of early-stage teams in Start-Up Chile using lean startup: hypothesis-based probing leads to more business idea changes, depending on team composition. Evidence on when MVP testing actually changes decisions.
course_use: Master reading on lean startup evidence; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Why the Lean Start-Up Changes Everything
author_source: Blank, S., Harvard Business Review 91(5), May 2013, article (practitioner)
note: Practitioner overview of lean startup: business model canvas, customer development, agile engineering and MVPs, contrasted with business plans. Short and the standard introductory text; HBR cover story.
course_use: Bachelor reading or flipped-classroom input before an MVP exercise; HBR paywall, EBSCO via WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Know Your Customers' Jobs to Be Done
author_source: Christensen, C.M., Hall, T., Dillon, K. & Duncan, D.S., Harvard Business Review 94(9), September 2016, article (practitioner)
note: Core text on Jobs-to-be-Done: customers hire products to make progress in a given circumstance and fire them if they perform poorly; includes functional, social and emotional dimensions of a job and the well-known milkshake example.
course_use: Bachelor/MBA reading; students write job statements for a product of their choice; HBR paywall, EBSCO via WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Turn Customer Input into Innovation
author_source: Ulwick, A.W., Harvard Business Review 80(1), 91-97, January 2002, article (practitioner)
note: Outcome-Driven Innovation: ask customers for desired outcomes, not solutions; rate importance and satisfaction and compute an opportunity score (Cordis angioplasty example). Quantitative JTBD method that fits a survey lab.
course_use: Lab: students run a small opportunity-score survey; HBR paywall, EBSCO via WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Conjoint Analysis in Marketing: New Developments with Implications for Research and Practice
author_source: Green, P.E. & Srinivasan, V., Journal of Marketing 54(4), 3-19, 1990, article
note: Standard review of conjoint for product design: attribute selection, data collection (full profile, hybrid, adaptive), estimation and market simulators for concept testing and share prediction. The 1978 JCR paper by the same authors (doi 10.1086/208721) covers the origins.
course_use: Background for a conjoint lab in concept testing (e.g. with Sawtooth or R); paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Pre-Test-Market Evaluation of New Packaged Goods: A Model and Measurement Method
author_source: Silk, A.J. & Urban, G.L., Journal of Marketing Research 15(2), 171-191, 1978, article
note: The ASSESSOR model: simulated store plus trial/repeat and preference models to forecast market share of a new packaged good before test market. Classic basis of today's simulated test markets (e.g. BASES).
course_use: Master session on forecasting; students recompute a trial-repeat share; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Pre-Test-Market Models: Validation and Managerial Implications
author_source: Urban, G.L. & Katz, G.M., Journal of Marketing Research 20(3), 221-234, 1983, article
note: Validation of ASSESSOR forecasts against actual test-market outcomes and the managerial value of pre-test markets in go/no-go decisions. Shows forecast accuracy in numbers.
course_use: Pair with Silk & Urban 1978; good for discussing forecast error; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Industrial New Product Launch Strategies and Product Development Performance
author_source: Hultink, E.J., Griffin, A., Hart, S. & Robben, H.S.J., Journal of Product Innovation Management 14(4), 243-257, 1997, article
note: Classifies strategic (innovativeness, targeting, timing) and tactical (pricing, promotion, distribution) launch decisions and links launch configurations to performance for industrial products.
course_use: Reading for the launch/go-to-market session; launch decision framework for student projects; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Externally Directed and Internally Directed Market Launch Management: The Role of Organizational Factors in Influencing New Product Success
author_source: Kuester, S., Homburg, C. & Hess, S.C., Journal of Product Innovation Management 29(S1), 38-52, 2012, article
note: Separates launch activities aimed at the market from those aimed at the own organisation (sales force, internal marketing) and shows internal launch management matters for success. German research team (Mannheim).
course_use: Master reading on launch; links to sales-force adoption of new products; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Impact of Market Orientation, Product Advantage, and Launch Proficiency on New Product Performance and Organizational Performance
author_source: Langerak, F., Hultink, E.J. & Robben, H.S.J., Journal of Product Innovation Management 21(2), 79-94, 2004, article
note: Manufacturing-firm sample: market orientation works through product advantage and launch proficiency on new product and firm performance. Connects marketing strategy with NPD outcomes.
course_use: Reading for market orientation and launch; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Effect of Market Orientation and Its Components on Innovation Consequences: A Meta-Analysis
author_source: Grinstein, A., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 36(2), 166-173, 2008, article (meta-analysis)
note: Meta-analysis showing market orientation and its components (customer and competitor orientation, interfunctional coordination) relate positively to innovation, with contextual moderators. Concise evidence base for market-driven innovation.
course_use: Short Master reading; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Cross-Functional Product Development Teams, Creativity, and the Innovativeness of New Consumer Products
author_source: Sethi, R., Smith, D.C. & Park, C.W., Journal of Marketing Research 38(1), 73-85, 2001, article
note: Consumer-product teams: superordinate identity, encouragement to take risks and customer influence increase innovativeness, while functional diversity per se does not. Nuances the 'just build a cross-functional team' advice.
course_use: Reading for the organising-for-innovation session; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Success Factors for Service Innovation: A Meta-Analysis
author_source: Storey, C., Cankurtaran, P., Papastathopoulou, P. & Hultink, E.J., Journal of Product Innovation Management 33(5), 527-548, 2016, article (meta-analysis)
note: Meta-analysis of service innovation success factors, compared with goods NPD; highlights front-line employees, customer involvement and service-specific process factors.
course_use: Reading for the service innovation session; pair with Henard & Szymanski; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Digital Innovation Management: Reinventing Innovation Management Research in a Digital World
author_source: Nambisan, S., Lyytinen, K., Majchrzak, A. & Song, M., MIS Quarterly 41(1), 223-238, 2017, article
note: Explains how digital products blur boundaries between product and process, between innovation stages, and of agency (platforms, layered modular architecture, continuous updates). Conceptual basis for digital product innovation.
course_use: Master background reading for digital product innovation; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Experimentation and Start-up Performance: Evidence from A/B Testing
author_source: Koning, R., Hasan, S. & Chatterji, A., Management Science 68(9), 6434-6453, 2022, article
note: Large panel of tech startups: adopting A/B testing tools is associated with better performance, more product launches and both incremental and more radical changes. Large-sample evidence for an experimentation culture in digital products.
course_use: Reading for digital product innovation and A/B testing culture; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Building a Culture of Experimentation
author_source: Thomke, S., Harvard Business Review 98(2), March-April 2020, article (practitioner)
note: Argues that behaviour and attitudes, not tools, limit business experimentation; principles include democratising testing across functions, data-driven decisions and treating failed tests as learning, with Booking.com as lead case. Companion to Thomke's book Experimentation Works (HBR Press 2020).
course_use: Bachelor/MBA reading for the digital-products session; HBR paywall, EBSCO via WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Product Design and Business Model Strategies for a Circular Economy
author_source: Bocken, N.M.P., de Pauw, I., Bakker, C. & van der Grinten, B., Journal of Industrial and Production Engineering 33(5), 308-320, 2016, article
note: Framework of slowing, closing and narrowing resource loops with matching design strategies (durability, design for disassembly, remanufacturing) and business models. Widely used framework for circular product innovation.
course_use: Reading and framework for a circular redesign exercise; open access

title: Success Factors for Environmentally Sustainable Product Innovation: A Meta-Analysis
author_source: Saeed, M.A. & Dangelico, R.M., Journal of Product Innovation Management 43(3), 539-570, 2026, article (meta-analysis)
note: Recent meta-analysis of drivers of environmentally sustainable product innovation success; lets students compare sustainable NPD success factors with the classic Henard & Szymanski list.
course_use: Master reading in the sustainability session; check OA, otherwise WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Mainstreaming Green Product Innovation: Why and How Companies Integrate Environmental Sustainability
author_source: Dangelico, R.M. & Pujari, D., Journal of Business Ethics 95(3), 471-486, 2010, article
note: Case-based study on drivers (regulation, market, values) and on how firms integrate environmental criteria across the product life cycle and into the NPD process. Accessible qualitative examples.
course_use: Bachelor/Master reading on green NPD; paid, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Product Design and Development (7th ed.)
author_source: Karl T. Ulrich, Steven D. Eppinger, Maria C. Yang; McGraw-Hill Education, 2020; textbook (ISBN 9781260043655)
note: Standard NPD text spanning engineering and marketing. Most useful chapters: development processes and organizations (Stage-Gate vs spiral/agile), opportunity identification, identifying customer needs (interview-to-needs-statement method), product specifications, concept generation, concept selection (Pugh screening and scoring matrices), concept testing (purchase-intent calibration), product architecture and platforms, prototyping, service design, product development economics (NPV model of a project). Exercises and templates per chapter. No German edition.
course_use: Core reading for the NPD-process, concept-testing and platform sessions. The concept-selection matrix works as an in-class lab. Paid (approx. 60-80 EUR; eBook via Connect); WU-Lizenz prüfen (McGraw-Hill eBook).

title: Innovation Management and New Product Development (7th ed.)
author_source: Paul Trott; Pearson, 2024 (copyright 2023-2026 depending on ISBN); textbook (ISBN 9781292251523 print, 9781292453620 eText)
note: Standard European business-school text linking innovation management and NPD. Part 1: innovation basics, national innovation systems, public-sector innovation. Part 2: IP, organisational knowledge, alliances, open innovation. Part 3 (NPD): product and brand strategy, NPD models (Stage-Gate, agile/hybrid), market research and its limits for radical innovation, managing the NPD team, packaging and launch. Each chapter ends with a case study, which gives a useful pool of cases.
course_use: Main textbook candidate for Bachelor/Master courses; end-of-chapter cases for seminar discussion. Paid (approx. 60-75 EUR); WU-Lizenz prüfen (Pearson eText).

title: Managing Innovation: Integrating Technological, Market and Organizational Change (8th ed.)
author_source: Joe Tidd, John Bessant; Wiley, Nov/Dec 2024 (imprint 2025); textbook, 672 pp. (ISBN 9781394252060)
note: Its process model of innovation (search, select, implement, capture value) is the strongest framework chapter. Also covers innovation types (incremental/radical, the 4Ps innovation space), sources of innovation including users and lead users, open innovation and networks, building the innovative organisation, creating new products and services, and measuring innovation (audit tool). The 7th ed. (2020) is still widely held in libraries.
course_use: Background reading for the innovation-types and innovation-process lectures; the 4Ps innovation space as a warm-up exercise. Paid (approx. 60 EUR). The O'Reilly link suggests the eBook is in O'Reilly Learning (WU-Lizenz prüfen).

title: New Products Management (12th ed.)
author_source: C. Merle Crawford, C. Anthony Di Benedetto; McGraw-Hill, 2021 (Connect release 2025); textbook, 18 chapters
note: NPD text from the marketing side, cut down to 18 chapters. Strong on opportunity identification and the product innovation charter, concept generation (attribute analysis, problem-based ideation), concept evaluation and testing, the full screen, sales forecasting and financial analysis (A-T-A-R model, purchase-intent adjustment), the product protocol, market testing (pseudo sale, test market), and launch planning and management. Good bridge to the pre-test-market and forecasting topics.
course_use: Core reading for the concept-testing, forecasting (A-T-A-R) and launch sessions; numerical A-T-A-R exercise. Paid (approx. 70-90 EUR); WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Strategic Management of Technological Innovation (7th ed.)
author_source: Melissa A. Schilling; McGraw-Hill, 2023 (ISE 9781265073350; a newer 7e printing with 2026 copyright exists); textbook, approx. 350 pp.
note: Strategy focus. Part 1, industry dynamics: sources of innovation, types and patterns incl. S-curves, standards battles and dominant design, timing of entry. Part 2, formulating strategy: choosing innovation projects (incl. real options and conjoint/screening), collaboration, protecting innovation. Part 3, implementation: organising, managing the NPD process (incl. Stage-Gate and QFD), NPD teams, deployment strategy and launch. The 7e adds six new short cases (e.g. Netflix and the streaming wars).
course_use: Reading for S-curves, platforms, timing of entry and launch; short cases for Master/MBA discussion. Paid (approx. 60-80 EUR); WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Winning at New Products: Creating Value Through Innovation (5th ed.)
author_source: Robert G. Cooper; Basic Books, 2017; practitioner textbook, approx. 450 pp. (ISBN 9780465093328)
note: Primary source for the Stage-Gate system, written by its author: success factors from NPD research, the stages and gates in detail, gate criteria and scoring models, portfolio management, and the next-generation Agile-Stage-Gate hybrid. Best text for success/failure factors and portfolio management. German translations of earlier editions are out of print, so use the English edition.
course_use: Core reading for the Stage-Gate and success-factor sessions; gate-scoring exercise on student project ideas. Paid (approx. 25-35 EUR).

title: Innovationsmanagement: Von der Idee zur erfolgreichen Vermarktung (6. Aufl.)
author_source: Dietmar Vahs, Alexander Brem, Christian Oswald; Schäffer-Poeschel, Oktober 2023; Lehrbuch, 651 S. (ISBN 978-3-7910-4278-7; ePDF 978-3-7910-4280-0)
note: Leading German-language textbook that follows the innovation process: Grundlagen und Innovationsarten, Innovationsstrategie, Ideengenerierung und Kreativitätstechniken, Ideenbewertung, Open Innovation, Umsetzung/F&E-Management, Markteinführung, Innovationscontrolling und -kennzahlen. Revised and expanded edition. Avoid unauthorised PDF copies online; use the publisher or a library.
course_use: German core reading for Bachelor courses taught in German; the Innovationscontrolling chapter for the KPI session. Paid (approx. 45 EUR); eBook WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Innovationsmanagement (7. Aufl.)
author_source: Jürgen Hauschildt, Sören Salomo, Carsten Schultz, Alexander Kock; Vahlen (Vahlens Handbücher), 2022/2023 (6. Aufl. 2016, ISBN 978-3-8006-4728-6)
note: Research-based German standard text, more academic than Vahs/Brem. Covers Innovationsbegriff und Innovationsgrad, Innovationsstrategie, Organisation (Promotoren-Modell), Innovationsprozess, Erfolgsfaktoren und Erfolgsmessung, Portfolio. Good source for defining radical vs incremental innovation (Innovationsgrad) and for the Promotoren-Modell. The 7th-edition ISBN and author list were not verified in search; check Vahlen or DNB.
course_use: Master-level background on innovation degree and success measurement. Paid (approx. 40 EUR); Vahlen eLibrary WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Business Model Navigator (2nd ed.)
author_source: Oliver Gassmann, Karolin Frankenberger, Michaela Choudury (Csik); FT Publishing/Pearson, 2020 (ISBN 9781292327129); German version: Geschäftsmodelle entwickeln (Hanser; current edition to be confirmed)
note: St. Gallen method for business-model innovation: 55+ business-model patterns, the magic triangle (who-what-how-value), and a four-step process (initiation, ideation, integration, implementation). The pattern cards transfer directly to workshop use. Useful for the digital/service product innovation and business-model topics.
course_use: Workshop tool where students recombine patterns for a product idea; reading for the business-model innovation session. Paid (approx. 30 EUR); WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The PDMA Handbook of Innovation and New Product Development (4th ed.)
author_source: Ludwig Bstieler, Charles H. Noble (eds.); Wiley/PDMA, 2023; handbook, 688 pp. (ISBN 9781119890218)
note: 32 new or refreshed chapters by academics and practitioners: front-end innovation, customer needs and user research, design thinking, agile and hybrid NPD, portfolio management, market forecasting, sustainable NPD, digital transformation of NPD, AI in NPD. Best single source for current practice and the PDMA vocabulary (also the basis of the NPDP certification). Individual chapters make good Master readings.
course_use: Chapter-level readings for Master/MBA (e.g. AI in NPD, forecasting, sustainability). Expensive in print; O'Reilly eBook WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail
author_source: Clayton M. Christensen; Harvard Business Review Press, 1997 (reissued 2016); German: The Innovator's Dilemma. Warum etablierte Unternehmen den Wettbewerb um bahnbrechende Innovationen verlieren (Vahlen)
note: Origin of the distinction between disruptive and sustaining innovation. The disk-drive and mechanical-excavator studies show how listening to the best customers leads incumbents to miss low-end and new-market disruption. Chapters 1-2 (disk drives, value networks) are enough for teaching. Still the standard reference although the theory is contested; pair with Christensen, Raynor and McDonald, HBR 2015, 'What is disruptive innovation?'.
course_use: Reading for the innovation-types session; debate exercise 'Is X disruptive?' (e.g. Tesla, Uber, ChatGPT). Paid (approx. 15-20 EUR).

title: Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
author_source: Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, David S. Duncan; Harper Business, 2016; German edition exists (title and publisher to be confirmed)
note: Accessible statement of Jobs-to-be-Done theory: the milkshake example, functional/social/emotional dimensions of a job, products being hired and fired. Complements Ulwick's outcome-driven version. Chapters 1-4 cover the theory; later chapters show how organisations implement it.
course_use: Reading for the JTBD session; students run JTBD switch interviews. Paid (approx. 20 EUR).

title: The Lean Startup
author_source: Eric Ries; Crown Business, 2011; German: Lean Startup. Schnell, risikolos und erfolgreich Unternehmen gründen (Redline)
note: Build-measure-learn loop, minimum viable product, validated learning, innovation accounting, pivot-or-persevere decisions. Parts 1-2 cover the concepts. Useful for contrasting lean/iterative development with Stage-Gate. The examples (IMVU, Dropbox, Zappos) are dated but well known.
course_use: Reading for the lean/agile NPD session; MVP design exercise. Paid (approx. 15-20 EUR).

title: Value Proposition Design
author_source: Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur, Gregory Bernarda, Alan Smith; Wiley, 2014; German: Value Proposition Design (Campus, 2015; to be confirmed)
note: The Value Proposition Canvas (customer jobs, pains and gains vs products, pain relievers and gain creators), fit concepts, and a toolbox of test cards and experiment types for testing ideas. Highly visual; many free canvas downloads on strategyzer.com.
course_use: Workshop/lab where student teams fill in the canvas for a product idea and design tests. Paid (approx. 30 EUR); canvases free.

title: Sprint: How to Solve Big Problems and Test New Ideas in Just Five Days
author_source: Jake Knapp, John Zeratsky, Braden Kowitz; Simon & Schuster / Bantam Press, 2016; German edition (Redline) to be confirmed
note: Google Ventures five-day design sprint: map, sketch, decide, prototype, test with five customers. The day-by-day checklists can be reused directly as a compressed course format.
course_use: Basis for a one- or two-day sprint workshop in class. Paid (approx. 15-20 EUR).

title: Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products that Create Customer Value and Business Value
author_source: Teresa Torres; Product Talk LLC, 2021; practitioner book
note: Current reference for product discovery in digital product teams: weekly customer interviews, the opportunity solution tree, assumption mapping and testing, the product trio (PM, designer, engineer). Best source for teaching discovery in software and digital products.
course_use: Reading for digital product innovation; opportunity solution tree exercise. Paid (approx. 25 EUR).

title: Inspired: How to Create Tech Products Customers Love (2nd ed.)
author_source: Marty Cagan; Wiley, 2018 (ISBN 9781119387503); German: Inspired, 2., vollst. überarb. Aufl., Wiley-VCH, 2022 (ISBN 9783527511051)
note: Silicon Valley Product Group view of product management: empowered product teams, product discovery vs delivery, prototype types (feasibility, user, live-data), product roadmaps and OKRs. Useful for digital product innovation and the role of the product manager.
course_use: Background reading for the digital product session or to prepare a guest talk. Paid (approx. 25 EUR).

title: Crossing the Chasm (3rd ed.)
author_source: Geoffrey A. Moore; Harper Business, 2014 (ISBN 9780062292988)
note: Technology adoption life cycle and the chasm between early adopters and the early majority; beachhead (D-Day) strategy, whole product, positioning. The 3rd ed. adds digital-era examples and two new appendices. Standard reference for adoption and launch of high-tech products.
course_use: Reading for the adoption and go-to-market session; students pick a beachhead segment for a tech product. Paid (approx. 15-20 EUR).

title: The Art of Innovation: Lessons in Creativity from IDEO
author_source: Tom Kelley, Jonathan Littman; Currency/Doubleday, 2001
note: IDEO's practice of observation, brainstorming rules, rapid prototyping and 'hot teams'; anecdotal but vivid. An older classic: for a current take, pair it with Kelley and Kelley 'Creative Confidence' (2013) or IDEO's free Field Guide to Human-Centered Design.
course_use: Optional background for the design-thinking and ideation sessions. Paid (approx. 15 EUR).

title: Jobs to be Done: Theory to Practice
author_source: Anthony W. Ulwick; Idea Bite Press/Strategyn, 2016 (ISBN 9780990576747)
note: Outcome-Driven Innovation: the job map, desired-outcome statements, the importance-satisfaction opportunity algorithm, and segmenting on unmet needs. Gives students a quantitative JTBD survey method they can replicate. Strategyn offers the e-book and audiobook free on its site.
course_use: Lab: write desired-outcome statements and score opportunities for a product category. Free e-book from Strategyn (avoid third-party PDF copies).

title: Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.)
author_source: Everett M. Rogers; Free Press (Simon & Schuster), 2003
note: Foundational theory of adoption: innovation attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability), adopter categories, the innovation-decision process, the S-curve of diffusion. Chapters 5-7 are the core for teaching. Still the standard reference cited in the Bass-model and Moore literature.
course_use: Background reading for the adoption/diffusion session; attribute-rating exercise. Paid (approx. 30 EUR); WU library copy likely.

title: Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI
author_source: Ethan Mollick; Portfolio/Penguin, 2024 (UK: WH Allen, ISBN 9780753560785); no German edition found
note: Short, accessible book on working with generative AI, in two parts: how AI systems work and how to use them in one's own work. Chapters treat AI as co-worker, co-teacher and creative partner, and introduce the 'jagged frontier' of AI capability. A good entry to the AI-in-product-innovation session.
course_use: Pre-reading for AI in product innovation; pair with a student exercise that generates and screens ideas with an LLM. Paid (approx. 20 EUR).

title: Entrepreneurship (OpenStax)
author_source: Michael Laverty, Chris Littel et al.; OpenStax (Rice University), 2020; open textbook, CC BY 4.0 (ISBN 9781947172708)
note: Free open textbook. Relevant chapters: Ch. 4 Creativity, Innovation, and Invention; Ch. 5 Identifying Entrepreneurial Opportunity; Ch. 6 Problem Solving and Need Recognition Techniques (creative problem solving, the Stanford design-thinking model, lean processes; links to the GV design sprint and IDEO Design Kit); Ch. 10 Launch for Growth to Success; Ch. 11 Business Model and Plan. US-centric and introductory. Also mirrored on LibreTexts.
course_use: Free pre-reading for Bachelor students (design thinking, opportunity identification); review questions usable as quiz items. Open access.

title: Principles of Marketing (OpenStax), Ch. 10 Product, Branding, and Packaging Decisions
author_source: OpenStax (Rice University), 2023; open textbook, CC BY
note: Chapter 10 covers the seven-stage new-product development process (idea generation, screening, concept development and testing, marketing strategy, business analysis, product development, test marketing), rewards and risks of NPD, reasons for success and failure, and evaluation metrics. Short, introductory and free.
course_use: Free entry reading for Bachelor students before the NPD-process lecture. Open access.

title: Free Innovation
author_source: Eric von Hippel; MIT Press, 2016 (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
note: Household-sector and user innovation: how consumers develop products for their own use and share them for free, survey evidence across countries, and how firms can build on free innovation. Strong background for lead users, user innovation and open innovation.
course_use: Master reading for the session on idea sources and lead users; free PDF. Open access.

title: Democratizing Innovation
author_source: Eric von Hippel; MIT Press, 2005 (free PDF under Creative Commons)
note: Classic statement of user innovation and the lead-user method, with chapters on lead users, why users share innovations, and toolkits for user innovation and design. Still the standard reference for the lead-user process. Free from the author's site.
course_use: Reading for the open-innovation/lead-user session; lead-user screening exercise. Free.

title: The Design Thinking Playbook / Das Design Thinking Playbook
author_source: Michael Lewrick, Patrick Link, Larry Leifer; Wiley, 2018 (English); German: Vahlen 2017, 2. überarb. Aufl. 2018 (Versus)
note: Practitioner playbook of the design-thinking process, mindset and methods (personas, empathy maps, prototyping, testing) with a running case. Later volumes (Toolbox, Launch) extend it to business ecosystems. German and English versions make it suitable for bilingual teaching; Swiss/German authors.
course_use: Workshop companion for the design-thinking sessions. Paid (approx. 30 EUR).

title: Principles of Marketing Engineering and Analytics (3rd ed.)
author_source: Gary L. Lilien, Arvind Rangaswamy, Arnaud De Bruyn; DecisionPro, 2017; textbook
note: Quantitative toolkit for the forecasting and testing part of the course: chapters on conjoint analysis, new-product forecasting with the Bass diffusion model, pre-test-market models (ASSESSOR logic), and new-product decision models, each with Excel-based software exercises.
course_use: Lab basis for Bass-model and conjoint exercises (Master). Paid; check WU library.

title: Monetizing Innovation: How Smart Companies Design the Product Around the Price
author_source: Madhavan Ramanujam, Georg Tacke; Wiley, 2016
note: Simon-Kucher authors argue that most innovation failures are monetization failures. Covers willingness-to-pay conversations early in NPD, segmentation and configuration (leaders, fillers, killers), and pricing models. Practice-based, from a German-founded firm (Simon-Kucher, Bonn).
course_use: Reading for the concept-testing and launch-pricing sessions; WTP interview exercise. Paid (approx. 25 EUR).

title: Experimentation Works: The Surprising Power of Business Experiments
author_source: Stefan H. Thomke; Harvard Business Review Press, 2020
note: Online A/B testing and business experimentation as an innovation capability (Booking.com, Microsoft): experiment design, and the culture and organisation needed for large-scale testing. Connects lean-startup ideas with rigorous testing in digital product innovation.
course_use: Master reading for the digital product experimentation session. Paid (approx. 25 EUR).

title: Most Innovative Companies 2025: In Disruptive Times, the Resilient Win
author_source: Boston Consulting Group (BCG); 26 June 2025; consulting report (19th annual innovation study)
note: Uses 20 years of BCG top-50 lists. Firms on the lists outperformed the market by about 2.4 pp TSR per year, but there is no consistent link between R&D spend and TSR. The share of executives who see their firm as an innovation leader fell 24 pp from 2021 to 2024, and only 3% of firms are in BCG's 'ready zone'. Chinese innovators have risen while Europe's share declined, and agentic AI is expected to speed up competition. Full PDF linked from the page.
course_use: Lecture opener on innovation and firm performance; class discussion of why R&D spend is not innovation output. Free.

title: Global Innovation 1000 (latest edition 2018)
author_source: Strategy& (PwC); annual study 2005-2018; consulting report and fact pack
note: Tracks the 1,000 largest corporate R&D spenders. The 2018 edition found R&D spending up 11.4% to USD 782 bn, with Amazon the top spender. Its recurring finding is that R&D spending and long-term financial performance are not correlated. Also classifies innovation strategies (need seekers, market readers, technology drivers). No edition after 2018 appeared in search, so treat it as a classic dataset rather than current figures.
course_use: Discussion of R&D intensity vs innovation success; fact-pack charts for slides. Free.

title: Oslo Manual 2018: Guidelines for Collecting, Reporting and Using Data on Innovation (4th ed.)
author_source: OECD/Eurostat; OECD Publishing, Paris / Eurostat, Luxembourg, 2018; DOI 10.1787/9789264304604-en
note: The international definitions behind all innovation statistics: product innovation vs business process innovation (the 2018 edition replaced the earlier four-type typology), the innovation-active firm, novelty levels (new to firm, market or world), object vs subject approach. Chapters 2-3 (concepts and definitions) are enough for teaching. Free to read on OECD iLibrary.
